name: TimescaleDB
tagline: PostgreSQL extension adding hypertables, columnar compression and continuous aggregates for time series.
description: TimescaleDB turns PostgreSQL into a time-series and real-time analytics database: hypertables partition data by time automatically, the hypercore engine converts older chunks into compressed columnar form, and continuous aggregates keep rollups incrementally up to date. Because it is an extension, you keep full SQL, joins, foreign keys and the rest of the Postgres ecosystem in the same database. Its developer renamed itself from Timescale to TigerData in June 2025 and sells the managed Tiger Cloud. The core is Apache-2.0, but compression, continuous aggregates and other advanced features sit under the source-available Timescale License, which bars offering them as a hosted DBaaS.

license.name: Apache-2.0 core + Timescale License (TSL) for advanced features

pricing.notes: Community edition (with TSL features) is free to self-host; Tiger Cloud bills compute and storage by usage.

managedServices.name: Azure Database for PostgreSQL (Apache-licensed TimescaleDB only)

scale.notes: One primary plus Postgres read replicas; the multi-node option was removed in 2.14. Tiger Cloud adds tiering of old chunks to object storage.

strengths: It is PostgreSQL: transactions, joins, foreign keys and every Postgres driver, ORM and BI tool work unchanged
Columnar compression of older chunks often shrinks storage by an order of magnitude
Continuous aggregates maintain rollups incrementally and can merge in not-yet-materialised recent data
Keeps time series next to relational business data, avoiding a second database
Automatic time partitioning with chunk-level retention and compression policies
weaknesses: Single-primary write path; write throughput is bounded by one server since multi-node was dropped
Compression and continuous aggregates are TSL-licensed, so third-party clouds only ship the Apache subset
Ingest at very high series cardinality trails purpose-built TSDBs
Updates and deletes on compressed chunks cost more than on row data
useCases: IoT and sensor data joined with relational metadata
Financial tick and market data analytics in SQL
Adding time-series analytics to an existing Postgres app
notIdealFor: Prometheus-scale metrics with millions of active series
Workloads that need horizontal write sharding
